name: Gather resources
summary: A unit earns money for its team by working the map instead of fighting. It mines ore, crystals or salvage from a field, or breaks down wrecks, and brings the haul to a drop-off (a refinery, a silo, a deployed base or a robot that follows the team), where it becomes team money. Some gatherers process on the spot by deploying beside the field, send out worker minions to do the digging, or warp home when full. The load is usually at risk until it is banked. The gatherer is either tough, like the Red Alert miners, or fragile, like the cheap Generals Workers and the Battlezone Scavengers, and weak in a fight either way. Its route, its field and its drop-off are all places the enemy can raid, so a team must decide how many players to spend on income and on escorts.
counterplay: Raid the gatherer away from its escort: it is slow and lightly armed or unarmed, and a kill before it banks also costs the team its load.
Kill the soft workers or haulers rather than the tough drop-off; the income stops until they are back.
Contest or deny the field: hold it, mine it out first, or cover it with mines or a hazard. Some fields run dry and need a long while to regrow.
Hit the bank: destroy the refinery or silo, or slip a spy or thief inside to steal what is stored there.
Use aircraft: most gatherers have nothing that shoots upward.
Deny salvage: destroy or reclaim wrecks yourself before the enemy's salvagers get to them.

other_examples.note: The two stock miners show the main twists. The Allied one drives out to the ore like any vehicle but teleports back to its refinery once full, so it spends little time on the road; it carries half as much and has no gun. The Soviet one drives both ways, carries twice the load, and defends itself with a machine gun that becomes a high-explosive auto-cannon at Elite rank.

other_examples.note: The plain version: an unarmed truck with very heavy armour that scoops ore or gems and hauls them to a refinery, built to survive a beating and get away. Every refinery comes with one, it can run soldiers over, and when it is destroyed its cargo bursts out and hurts infantry around it.

sources.title: Ore truck, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Its quote box copies the Red Alert manual entry.

other_examples.unit: Supply gathering (Chinooks, supply trucks and GLA Workers)
other_examples.note: Boxes of supplies sit in docks around the map, and each side carries them to its own supply building with a different hauler: US helicopters, Chinese trucks, or GLA Workers on foot, who are cheap, carry less per trip and also build, repair and clear mines. Docks run dry, so every side also has a slower second income, and some units steal money from the enemy's supply buildings instead.

other_examples.unit: Reclaim (engineers, command units and a few combat units)
other_examples.note: The salvage version: builders break wrecks, rocks and trees down into the game's two resources, and a fresh wreck pays back most of what the dead unit cost unless it is shot up further. Units on patrol reclaim whatever they pass by themselves. Living enemy units can be reclaimed too, for nothing, which engineers use to fend off enemy engineers and scouts.

A summoned worker: a base building drops a mining robot anywhere the player can see. It brings back far more per trip than a normal worker, shuts down after about a minute, and can patch up damaged machines in a pinch.

shooter_analogues.note: A player-driven mining truck aims a laser at a crystal and holds fire to fill its tank, then pours the load into silos or a Colossus tank, or deploys so the team can build base structures from it. A mineral radar points it to deposits, and the driver can also burn the stored load on a barrier or a turbo boost.

Any soldier can hammer the nodes of a salvage field, carry the salvage in their own inventory and have it turned into other materials at a refinery; heavier tools and harvesters mine faster. A mined node is replaced from the field's reserve a few seconds later, and an exhausted field only comes back after a long wait.

Players dig minerals into their own inventory, but the haul only counts for the team once it is deposited into a walking robot that follows the squad and comes to a marked spot when called. The robot itself can't be hurt, so the danger is on the miners.

In this game the player both drives a combat vehicle and commands a base. Scavengers roam by themselves to scoop up scrap from wrecks and deposits and take it home to the base; they are lightly armoured and run when shot at. The player can also take the controls of one, pick scrap up with a key and unload it by driving next to a silo.

sources.title: Bio-metal Scavenging, Battlezone Wiki
sources.note: The training mission that introduces the command interface, the Recycler and the Scavenger, which must be guarded because it has no weapons.

player_translation.summary: A tough, nearly harmless economy unit that earns money for the whole team by working a node and banking the haul. Its player trades kills for income: picking safe or rich fields, timing runs home and calling for escorts, while enemy raiders treat it as a prize.
as_user: You buy a slow, tough hauler and spend the life on the economy: drive to a node, hold the mining tool on it to fill your hopper, then drive into a drop-off's ring to bank the load. Every load adds to the team's money, and the scoreboard credits you with the income.
Until you bank it, the load is yours to lose: if you die on the way home it spills as a pickup the enemy can take, so you judge when a half-full hopper is worth the trip.
Safe nodes near your base pay little and rich ones sit in contested ground. Your light self-defence gun scares off a lone raider but loses any real fight, so you call for help early.
With the worker-crew variant you park and deploy beside the field instead: AI workers do the digging and the walking, and your job is to keep the spot safe and stay alive.
as_target: A gatherer is a raid prize: killing it costs the enemy income and drops its load for you. It is tough, so bring focus fire or anti-armour and catch it away from its escort.
Watch the nodes and the routes to the drop-offs; standing on a node, or mining it out first, starves the other team.
Workers and haulers are the soft part: kill them to stop the money, then deal with the master or the bank.
teammates: Escorts get a clear job: ride along the route, and bring anti-air and anti-raider picks.
Everyone gains from the shared income, which lets the whole team buy better units sooner, so the team agrees on how many players to spend on the economy.
Repair players keep the tough hauler going, and a transport can carry a worker-crew gatherer to a far field.
On the enemy side, raiders, aircraft and infiltrators get a target worth hunting.
controls: Move with WASD and aim with the mouse; left mouse fires the light self-defence gun.
Hold right mouse on the node under the cursor to mine; the hopper meter fills while you hold. This is the pattern's one counted key.
Banking needs no key: drive into a drop-off's ring and the load is paid in. Variants put their own key on Q instead: deploy beside the field, call down a worker or warp home.
Middle mouse, the universal ping, marks 'escort me' or 'node contested'.
feedback: A hopper meter on the HUD and a visible load on the vehicle that grows as it fills, so a full hauler is obvious from above.
Team-coloured rings around nodes and drop-offs, showing each node's remaining yield and its regrow timer.
A coin sound and a money pop on banking, shown to the whole team, and a 'load lost' line in the kill feed when a gatherer dies full.
Minimap icons for nodes, contested nodes and gatherers under attack.
changes_from_rts: In the RTS the miner works on its own while the player runs a base; here a person drives it, so runs must be short and full of small choices (which node, when to bank) or the job turns into a chore.
Income has to reach teammates and credit the gatherer, through a share or score, or nobody will give up fighting to play it.
Red Alert's miners are very tough and often immune to control effects; keep the hauler tough but give raiders a reachable prize: the load, the workers or the bank.
One gatherer must not decide a match: cap each node's yield, let fields run dry and regrow, and give each extra gatherer on a team less than the last.
The RTS refinery is a base building; here drop-offs are map points or deployables, so map design sets the economy.
Loads spill as pickups instead of vanishing with the vehicle, so a raid pays the raider.

team_play.notes: The gatherer is valuable to the whole team but helpless alone: teams decide how many players to spend on income and escorts, raiders get a prize, and a well-guarded hauler can lure raiders into an ambush.

notes: Needs a match economy: a team money pool or shares, income credited per player, and buying that responds mid-match.
Nodes, drop-off rings, a hopper meter and dropped loads as pickups are simple; placing nodes and routes is map-design work.
The worker-crew variant adds AI workers that walk between field and drop-off, plus their replacement.
Income against combat value needs tuning with match data.
Snowballing: the team with more income buys more and wins more fights; cap yields and damp extra gatherers.
Passive farming: a player can mine safe nodes and add little to the fight; tie the best rewards to contested nodes.
Too weak or dull and nobody picks it; too strong and every team is forced to field one.
A full hauler and an empty one must look different from above.
Players must see which nodes are contested, which drop-off belongs to whom and how much a node has left.
AI workers must look different from enemy players so nobody mistakes them for a threat.

variants.name: Haul and bank
variants.summary: Mine a node with a held tool, carry the load in a hopper and bank it at a drop-off; dying before banking spills the load.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 1 Ore Truck, Red Alert 2 War Miner, PlanetSide 2 ANT, Battlezone Scavenger

variants.name: Warp home when full
variants.summary: Drives out like any vehicle but teleports straight back to the drop-off once full, so it can be caught only on the way out or at the field, never on the trip home (and it can be ordered to warp home early to escape an attack); the price is a smaller load and no gun.

variants.name: Deploy beside the field
variants.summary: Deploys next to the field and becomes its own drop-off, so there is no route to raid; while deployed it can't move and becomes the target.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2: Yuri's Revenge Slave Miner

adds_weaknesses.why: Spends its life mining instead of fighting, and deployed it can't move, so a raid that reaches the field hits the whole income at once.

variants.name: Worker crew
variants.summary: Fields a few AI workers that dig and carry for it instead of mining itself. The workers are soft, so the enemy can kill them to cut the income; lost ones come back as in reinforce-squad's respawning-followers variant.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2: Yuri's Revenge Slave Miner (free slaves); Generals GLA Workers (bought one by one)

variants.name: Salvage wrecks
variants.summary: The battlefield is the field: it breaks down wrecks, and rocks or trees where the map has them, into money, so every fight leaves salvage and players can deny it by destroying wrecks first. Unlike leech-weapon-on-kill, the pay is team money from any wreck, salvaged by holding the tool on it, not a claim on a kill the unit made.
variants.seen_in: Supreme Commander reclaim; Battlezone scavengers collecting scrap from downed vehicles

variants.name: Call down a worker
variants.summary: On a key, drop a temporary worker robot at a node you can see; it mines faster than a player for a short time, then shuts down, and enemies can shoot it.

variants.name: Mobile drop-off
variants.summary: The unit is the bank: teammates bring their loads to it wherever it stands, and it carries the team's unbanked haul until it cashes in.
variants.seen_in: Deep Rock Galactic M.U.L.E., a robot the team calls over to deposit minerals

adds_strengths.why: Teammates bank their loads into it wherever it stands, so nobody has to make the trip home.

adds_weaknesses.why: It carries the whole team's unbanked haul, so losing it loses everyone's loads.

variants.name: Spend the haul
variants.summary: The gatherer can burn its own stored load to power a barrier or a speed boost, so it chooses between banking the money and surviving the trip.
variants.seen_in: PlanetSide 2 ANT, whose stored cortium powers a barrier or a turbo

adds_strengths.why: Earns money for the whole team by working nodes or wrecks, so the team can buy better units sooner.

adds_weaknesses.why: Spends its life mining instead of fighting, risks its load until it banks it, and is helpless against raiders without an escort.

countered_by.why: Fast flankers catch it on the way home, kill it away from its escort and take or destroy its load.
Most gatherers have nothing that shoots upward, so aircraft raid them freely.
Spies and thieves slip into the drop-off and steal the banked money.

open_questions: Is money in Shamble Frontlines shared by the team or kept per player? A gatherer only works if its income reaches teammates.
Should unbanked loads spill as pickups for the killer, or simply vanish?
Do the maps get resource nodes and drop-offs, or is salvage from wrecks the only source?
How many gatherers per team before income stops scaling: a cap per node, a cap per team, or shrinking returns?

For the merge pass: leech-weapon-on-kill's loot-currency variant (wrecks pay out resources or crafting material) and its Supreme Commander Reclaim example cover the same mechanic as salvage-wrecks and this pattern's Reclaim example: the same interaction, the same counterplay (deny or destroy the wrecks) and the same source. research/registry-notes/patterns.md also folds reclaiming wrecks into gather-resources. Recommendation: fold both into salvage-wrecks, and keep in leech-weapon-on-kill only what a unit takes for itself from a kill it claimed. Writers never edit an existing pattern file, so the merge pass makes the change; it should also decide whether the variant's other seen_in, ARC Raiders salvage, moves with it.

shooter_fit.reason: Proven in team shooters that have a match economy (PlanetSide 2, Foxhole), but it takes a player out of the fight and needs nodes, a shared money pool and anti-snowball caps to stay fun and fair.

review.notes: Re-checked field by field against its sources by the batch r1 checker, which covered all 33 batch patterns; research/r1/checker/checks.json lists every field and verdict. Nothing was found wrong.
